## Sparse Neighbourhoods Can Fall Silent

<div class="matrix-grid">
  <div class="matrix-head"></div><div class="matrix-head">Item A</div><div class="matrix-head">Item B</div><div class="matrix-head">Item C</div><div class="matrix-head">Item D</div>
  <div class="matrix-head">User 1</div><div class="matrix-rated">5</div><div class="matrix-rated">4</div><div class="matrix-missing">—</div><div class="matrix-missing">—</div>
  <div class="matrix-head">User 2</div><div class="matrix-missing">—</div><div class="matrix-rated">5</div><div class="matrix-rated">4</div><div class="matrix-missing">—</div>
  <div class="matrix-head">User 3</div><div class="matrix-rated">4</div><div class="matrix-missing">—</div><div class="matrix-missing">—</div><div class="matrix-rated">5</div>
  <div class="matrix-head">Target user</div><div class="matrix-rated">5</div><div class="matrix-missing">—</div><div class="matrix-target">?</div><div class="matrix-missing">—</div>
</div>


::: notes
Ask students to identify the Week 01 bottleneck: few co-rated items can make a local similarity estimate unstable or unavailable. Do not claim that factorisation removes missingness.
:::

## Global Patterns Remain in the Matrix

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="48%"}
### Neighbourhood CF

- Starts with local overlap.
- Compares named rows or columns.
- Can be silent when overlap is thin.
:::
::: {.column width="48%"}
### Latent-factor model

- Learns shared coordinates from many interactions.
- Uses global patterns to score a user–item pair.
- Still inherits the limits of its evidence.
:::
:::

::: {.callout-tip .to-think-about title="To think about"}
Does a learned representation make a missing interaction more trustworthy—or only make a prediction possible?
:::

::: notes
The intended answer: it makes a prediction possible by exploiting patterns elsewhere; it does not convert a missing observation into ground truth.
:::

# 02 Information Retrieval Fundamentals {background-color="#EF7C00"}

## Text Becomes Searchable as a Vector
::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="47%"}
### Query
`feline care`

A query is a short text representation of an information need.
:::
::: {.column width="6%"}
<div style="font-size:2.2em;text-align:center;padding-top:1.1em;color:#EF7C00;">→</div>
:::
::: {.column width="47%"}
### Item description
`cat health guide`

An item can be represented in the same feature space for comparison.
:::
:::

> **Information retrieval (IR)** asks which available documents or items best satisfy a text-based need.

::: notes
Bridge from the protected neighbourhood-CF slides: both retrieval and recommendation need a representation before they can compute a score. The evidence differs: words for IR, interaction history for collaborative filtering.
[Sources]
- Manning, C. D., Raghavan, P., & Schütze, H. (2008). *Introduction to Information Retrieval*, Chapter 6.
:::

## A Bag of Words Is Sparse and Literal

<div class="matrix-grid" style="grid-template-columns:1.4fr repeat(5, .8fr);font-size:.82em;">
  <div class="matrix-head">text / term</div><div class="matrix-head">cat</div><div class="matrix-head">feline</div><div class="matrix-head">health</div><div  lass="matrix-head">care</div><div class="matrix-head">guide</div>
  <div class="matrix-head">query: feline care</div><div class="matrix-missing">0</div><div class="matrix-target">1</div><div class="matrix-missing">0</div><div class="matrix-target">1</div><div class="matrix-missing">0</div>
  <div class="matrix-head">doc: cat health guide</div><div class="matrix-target">1</div><div class="matrix-missing">0</div><div class="matrix-target">1</div><div class="matrix-missing">0</div><div class="matrix-target">1</div>
</div>

- One coordinate per vocabulary term; most coordinates are zero.
- Word order is discarded, but exact lexical evidence is retained.
- `cat` and `feline` occupy different coordinates unless we add another mechanism.

::: notes
Use the grid to make sparsity visible. This is intentionally a representation, not yet a claim that it understands meaning.
[Sources]
- Manning, C. D., Raghavan, P., & Schütze, H. (2008). *Introduction to Information Retrieval*, Chapters 1 and 6.
:::

## TF and IDF Signal Different Things

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="47%"}
### TF: local evidence
$$
\operatorname{tf}(t,d)=\text{count of term }t\text{ in document }d
$$

Repeated occurrence can strengthen a term's contribution **within one document**.
:::
::: {.column width="47%"}
### IDF: collection discrimination
$$
\operatorname{idf}(t)=\log\frac{N}{df_t}
$$

A term found in almost every document contributes less to distinguishing documents.
:::
:::

$$
\operatorname{tf\!\mbox{-}\!idf}(t,d)=\operatorname{tf}(t,d)\times\operatorname{idf}(t)
$$

::: notes
Emphasise that IDF is a collection-level property while TF is document-specific. Do not say a high frequency word is always irrelevant; it is simply less discriminative if it appears everywhere.
[Sources]
- Manning, C. D., Raghavan, P., & Schütze, H. (2008). *Introduction to Information Retrieval*, Chapter 6.
:::

## Worked TF–IDF: Rank a Query Match

**Query:** `machine learning`

| Term | TF in guide A | IDF | Weight in guide A |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| `machine` | 2 | 1.2 | 2.4 |
| `learning` | 1 | 1.6 | 1.6 |

<div class="factor-flow" style="margin-top:.6em;">
  <div class="factor-card"><strong>Query vector</strong><br>Weights the terms that express the need.</div>
  <div class="factor-arrow">·</div>
  <div class="factor-card"><strong>Document vector</strong><br>Weights the same vocabulary coordinates.</div>
  <div class="factor-arrow">→</div>
  <div class="factor-card"><strong>Cosine score</strong><br>Ranks documents by directional alignment.</div>
</div>

A vector-space retriever ranks **lexical evidence**; it has not yet inferred that different words can express a similar idea.

::: notes
Do not calculate a full cosine normalisation by hand. The goal is to identify what determines a contribution to the score, then introduce cosine as a scale-aware comparison.
[Sources]
- Manning, C. D., Raghavan, P., & Schütze, H. (2008). *Introduction to Information Retrieval*, Chapter 6.
:::

## Dense Word Embeddings Learn Neighbourhoods

<div class="factor-flow">
  <div class="factor-card"><strong>Training contexts</strong><br>Words that occur in related contexts provide a learning signal.</div>
  <div class="factor-arrow">→</div>
  <div class="factor-card"><strong>Dense vectors</strong><br>Each word receives a short, continuous learned representation.</div>
  <div class="factor-arrow">→</div>
  <div class="factor-card"><strong>Neighbourhoods</strong><br>Related usage can place vectors closer together.</div>
</div>

- Dense vectors have far fewer dimensions than a vocabulary-sized bag-of-words vector.
- They can support semantic generalisation such as related wording.
- Their coordinates are learned patterns, **not human-readable facts or ground truth**.

::: notes
Introduce word2vec as an historically influential example, not as the only embedding approach. State the limitation: a single static vector cannot solve every context, phrase, ambiguity, or bias issue.
[Sources]
- Mikolov, T. et al. (2013). “Efficient Estimation of Word Representations in Vector Space.”
- Mikolov, T. et al. (2013). “Distributed Representations of Words and Phrases and their Compositionality.”
:::

## Sparse and Dense Make Different Trade-offs

| Question | TF–IDF | Dense word embedding |
|---|---|---|
| What is represented? | Exact vocabulary-term evidence | Learned continuous coordinates |
| Main strength | Transparent lexical matching | Can generalise across related usage |
| Main limitation | Synonyms remain separate terms | Learned proximity can be opaque or misleading |
| Typical score | Cosine similarity over sparse vectors | Cosine/dot-product similarity over dense vectors |

> **Bridge:** IR turns **text into comparable vectors**. LFM will turn **interaction history into comparable user and item vectors**.

::: notes
This comparison is the central bridge. Avoid presenting dense embeddings as a universal upgrade: retrieval systems commonly combine sparse and dense signals.
[Sources]
- Manning, C. D., Raghavan, P., & Schütze, H. (2008). *Introduction to Information Retrieval*.
- Mikolov, T. et al. (2013). “Efficient Estimation of Word Representations in Vector Space.”
:::

## 🎰 Bandit Time: Where Does TF–IDF Struggle? {background-color="#003D7C"}

<p class="bandit-question"><strong>A query is “feline care”. A useful document says “cat health”. Why can a conventional TF–IDF cosine score under-rank it?</strong></p>
<div class="bandit-options">
  <div class="bandit-option" style="border-color:#D32F2F"><strong>A.</strong> TF–IDF forbids any document from receiving more than one score.</div>
  <div class="bandit-option" style="border-color:#1976D2"><strong>B.</strong> <code>feline</code> and <code>cat</code> are separate vocabulary dimensions unless a mechanism connects them.</div>
  <div class="bandit-option" style="border-color:#388E3C"><strong>C.</strong> Cosine similarity can only compare dense vectors.</div>
  <div class="bandit-option" style="border-color:#7B1FA2"><strong>D.</strong> IDF removes every rare word from the query.</div>
</div>
<p style="margin-top:.7em;color:#80cbc4;font-size:.73em;">Answer: <strong style="color:#ffffff;">B</strong>. TF–IDF rewards shared lexical coordinates; embeddings can help relate wording, but they introduce a different modelling assumption.</p>
::: notes
MCQ. Invite individual answers first, then ask for one rationale. The key distinction is lexical mismatch, not a claim that dense embeddings are always correct.
:::

```{=html}
<script>
(function () {
  var TOTAL = 5 * 60, remaining = TOTAL, interval = null, state = 'idle', audioContext = null;
  var textEl = document.getElementById('timer-text-w02ir');
  var statusEl = document.getElementById('timer-status-w02ir');
  var ringEl = document.getElementById('donut-ring-w02ir');
  var buttonEl = document.getElementById('break-btn-w02ir');
  var circumference = 2 * Math.PI * 75;
  function pad(v) { return v < 10 ? '0' + v : '' + v; }
  function render() {
    var display = pad(Math.floor(remaining / 60)) + ':' + pad(remaining % 60);
    textEl.textContent = display;
    statusEl.textContent = state === 'complete' ? "Time's up!" : display;
    ringEl.setAttribute('stroke-dashoffset', circumference * (1 - remaining / TOTAL));
  }
  function ring() {
    if (!audioContext) return;
    var oscillator = audioContext.createOscillator(), gain = audioContext.createGain(), now = audioContext.currentTime;
    oscillator.type = 'sine'; oscillator.frequency.value = 880;
    gain.gain.setValueAtTime(.18, now); gain.gain.exponentialRampToValueAtTime(.001, now + .5);
    oscillator.connect(gain); gain.connect(audioContext.destination); oscillator.start(now); oscillator.stop(now + .5);
  }
  function pause() {
    if (state !== 'running') return;
    clearInterval(interval); interval = null; state = 'paused'; buttonEl.textContent = '▶ Resume';
  }
  function reset() {
    clearInterval(interval); interval = null; remaining = TOTAL; state = 'idle';
    ringEl.setAttribute('stroke', '#EF7C00'); buttonEl.textContent = '▶ Start Timer'; render();
  }
  function tick() {
    remaining = Math.max(0, remaining - 1); render();
    if (remaining === 0) { clearInterval(interval); interval = null; state = 'complete'; ringEl.setAttribute('stroke', '#00c875'); buttonEl.textContent = '↻ Restart Timer'; ring(); }
  }
  buttonEl.addEventListener('click', function () {
    if (state === 'complete') { reset(); return; }
    if (state === 'running') { pause(); return; }
    var AudioContextClass = window.AudioContext || window.webkitAudioContext;
    if (AudioContextClass && !audioContext) audioContext = new AudioContextClass();
    if (audioContext && audioContext.state === 'suspended') audioContext.resume();
    state = 'running'; buttonEl.textContent = '⏸ Pause'; interval = setInterval(tick, 1000);
  });
  render();
  window._cpTimers = window._cpTimers || {};
  document.addEventListener('DOMContentLoaded', function () {
    function bindReveal() {
      if (typeof Reveal === 'undefined' || !Reveal.isReady || !Reveal.isReady()) { setTimeout(bindReveal, 200); return; }
      var slideEl = buttonEl.closest('section');
      var allSlides = Array.prototype.slice.call(document.querySelectorAll('.reveal .slides > section'));
      var slideIndex = allSlides.indexOf(slideEl);
      if (slideIndex >= 0) window._cpTimers[slideIndex] = pause;
      Reveal.on('slidechanged', function (event) {
        var previousIndex = allSlides.indexOf(event.previousSlide);
        if (previousIndex >= 0 && window._cpTimers[previousIndex]) window._cpTimers[previousIndex]();
      });
    }
    bindReveal();
  });
})();

</script>
```


::: notes
Break slide. Start the timer when announcing the break. KWIC fact source: Hallam Stevens, “Hans Peter Luhn and the Birth of the Hashing Algorithm,” *IEEE Spectrum* (2018).
:::

# 03 Latent Factor Models {background-color="#EF7C00"}

## One Vector-Space Idea, Two Evidence Sources

| Retrieval | Latent-factor recommendation |
|---|---|
| Query and document vectors | User and item vectors |
| Evidence: words in text | Evidence: observed interactions |
| Score: lexical/semantic match | Score: predicted affinity |
| Goal: rank relevant documents | Goal: rank plausible items |

> **Analogy, not equivalence:** a latent factor is not a word, a recorded metadata field, or a fact about a person.

::: notes
Use the preceding IR section to make LFM less mysterious. The geometry is analogous: represent objects in a common vector space, then score a relationship. The data-generating processes and interpretations are different.
:::

## Factorisation Learns Shared Coordinates

$$
R \approx P Q^\top
$$

<div class="factor-flow">
  <div class="factor-card"><strong>Interaction matrix \(R\)</strong><br>Observed user–item feedback with many blanks.</div>
  <div class="factor-arrow">≈</div>
  <div class="factor-card"><strong>User matrix \(P\)</strong><br>One learned vector per user.</div>
  <div class="factor-arrow">×</div>
  <div class="factor-card"><strong>Item matrix \(Q\)</strong><br>One learned vector per item.</div>
</div>

A compact set of learned coordinates can capture recurring interaction patterns that local neighbourhoods may miss.

::: notes
Re-use the distinction from the protected slides: LFM makes a prediction possible from distributed patterns; it does not turn a missing interaction into ground truth.
[Sources]
- Koren, Y., Bell, R., & Volinsky, C. (2009). “Matrix Factorization Techniques for Recommender Systems.” *Computer*, 42(8), 30–37.
:::

## Factors Are Patterns, Not Personal Facts

| Tempting shortcut | Better statement |
|---|---|
| “Dimension 3 is this user’s identity.” | Dimension 3 is a learned coordinate associated with interaction patterns. |
| “The factor is a hidden genre tag.” | A factor may correlate with metadata, but it is inferred rather than recorded. |
| “The factor explains the person.” | The factor supports a score under a particular dataset and objective. |

::: notes
Retain this language discipline. It applies equally to dense word embeddings: a useful coordinate system is not an ontological truth.
:::

## A Dot Product Turns Factors into a Score

$$
\hat r_{ui}=p_u^\top q_i
$$

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="48%"}
### User vector
$$
p_u=[p_{u1},p_{u2},\ldots,p_{uk}]
$$
A learned location in the model’s preference space.
:::
::: {.column width="48%"}
### Item vector
$$
q_i=[q_{i1},q_{i2},\ldots,q_{ik}]
$$
How an item aligns with the learned interaction patterns.
:::
:::

The dot product produces a **model score**. A production recommender can still filter, diversify, or re-rank the resulting candidates.

::: notes
Make the bridge to cosine from IR carefully: both use vector geometry, but the factor score is learned from interactions and need not be normalised like a retrieval cosine.
:::

## Worked Calculation: Two Items, One Score

$$
p_u=[0.8,0.2], \qquad q_A=[0.9,0.1], \qquad q_B=[0.4,0.8]
$$

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="48%"}
### Item A
$$
\hat r_{uA}=0.8(0.9)+0.2(0.1)=\mathbf{0.74}
$$
:::
::: {.column width="48%"}
### Item B
$$
\hat r_{uB}=0.8(0.4)+0.2(0.8)=\mathbf{0.48}
$$
:::
:::

**Current model verdict:** Item A scores higher.
**Still unresolved:** diversity, constraints, uncertainty, exposure, and the rest of the candidate list.

::: notes
Ask students to verify each product before showing the totals. Reiterate that score comparison is not a full ranking policy.
:::

## Training Fits Evidence, Regularisation Limits It

$$
\min_{P,Q}\; \sum_{(u,i)\in\Omega}(r_{ui}-p_u^\top q_i)^2 + \lambda\left(\lVert P\rVert_F^2+\lVert Q\rVert_F^2\right)
$$

- **Explicit feedback:** a rating can support a prediction-error loss.
- **Implicit feedback:** an interaction supports relative or binary preference evidence.
- **Regularisation:** discourages a model that memorises the observed matrix too conveniently.

::: notes
Explain the equation qualitatively. The objective and sampling scheme are design choices, not generic facts about user preference.
[Sources]
- Koren, Y., Bell, R., & Volinsky, C. (2009). “Matrix Factorization Techniques for Recommender Systems.”
:::

## BPR Makes LFM Ranking-Aware

$$
\log \sigma\big(s(u,i)-s(u,j)\big)
$$

<div class="factor-flow">
  <div class="factor-card"><strong>Observed item \(i\)</strong><br>User \(u\) watched, clicked, or purchased it.</div>
  <div class="factor-arrow">&gt;</div>
  <div class="factor-card"><strong>Sampled item \(j\)</strong><br>An unobserved alternative for that user.</div>
  <div class="factor-arrow">→</div>
  <div class="factor-card"><strong>Pairwise loss</strong><br>Reward \(i\) being ranked above \(j\).</div>
</div>

> **BPR is not a neural architecture.** It is a pairwise ranking objective commonly used with LFM-style user and item factors.

::: notes
Name BPR in full: Bayesian Personalized Ranking. Contrast the same latent-factor representation with a different learning objective: numeric prediction versus relative ranking under implicit feedback.
[Sources]
- Rendle, S. et al. (2009). “BPR: Bayesian Personalized Ranking from Implicit Feedback.”
:::

## Choose Code That Matches the Evidence

| Method | Library | Evidence and pedagogical role |
|---|---|---|
| **Regularised MF / SVD** | Surprise `SVD` | Explicit ratings; prediction-style factor baseline. |
| **BPR-MF** | RecBole `BPR` | Implicit interactions; **primary worked example** for top-*K* ranking. |
| **Implicit ALS** | `implicit` | Confidence-weighted sparse implicit feedback; comparison extension. |
| **NMF** | scikit-learn or Surprise `NMF` | Non-negative-factorisation constraint; extension code. |
| **NeuMF** | RecBole `NeuMF` | Neural interaction model; preview only, not BPR itself. |

::: notes
Explain that “SVD” in practical recommender libraries normally means a regularised latent-factor model trained iteratively, not applying one literal SVD to a sparse ratings matrix. RecBole supports BPR and NeuMF; classic SVD and NMF should use a separate library.
:::

## 👥 Activity 1: Choose the Baseline, Defend the Match {background-color="#003D7C"}

<p class="activity-question"><strong>Work in pairs.</strong> For one of the cases, choose a first LFM-related baseline. Produce: <em>evidence → method → ranking/prediction metric → one limitation</em>.</p>
<div class="activity-grid">
  <div class="activity-card"><h3>Movie ratings</h3>Users give 1–5 star ratings. Is the score itself the target?</div>
  <div class="activity-card"><h3>Podcast listens</h3>Users either listened or did not. Which ranked-list outcome matters?</div>
  <div class="activity-card"><h3>Music discovery</h3>Interactions are implicit and exposure is uneven. What needs monitoring beyond relevance?</div>
</div>
<div class="activity-output"><strong>Produce:</strong> one defensible method/metric pair and one assumption that could make the baseline misleading.</div>

::: notes
Student activity. Invite two contrasting reports. One correct family of answers: explicit ratings → regularised MF/SVD → RMSE/MAE; implicit listens → BPR-MF → NDCG@K/Recall@K. Ask why neither metric establishes causal user value.
:::

## Worked RecBole Example: BPR on MovieLens 100K

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="56%"}
<div class="code-panel"><pre style="margin:0;color:inherit;"># test.yaml
USER_ID_FIELD: user_id
ITEM_ID_FIELD: item_id
load_col:
  inter: [user_id, item_id]
embedding_size: 64
epochs: 500
metrics: ['Recall', 'MRR', 'NDCG']
topk: 10

# run.py
from recbole.quick_start import run_recbole
run_recbole(model='BPR', dataset='ml-100k',
            config_file_list=['test.yaml'])</pre></div>
:::
::: {.column width="39%"}
### What is happening?
- RecBole loads user–item interactions.
- `BPR` learns user/item factors with a pairwise ranking loss.
- `embedding_size` sets the factor dimension.
- Ranking metrics evaluate the declared held-out protocol.
:::
:::

::: notes
Present this as a compact reproducible configuration—not a live installation exercise. Ask students to identify the evidence used (interactions, not text or explicit ratings) and the objective (ranked-list quality).
[Sources]
- RecBole documentation, “BPR.” https://recbole.io/docs/user_guide/model/general/bpr.html
:::

## Read Model Output as Limited Evidence

| Output artefact | What it can support | What it cannot establish alone |
|---|---|---|
| Training loss | Whether the stated loss changes during optimisation. | Real-world user value or fairness. |
| Recall@10 / NDCG@10 | A ranking comparison under the declared held-out protocol. | A production outcome without further evaluation. |
| Top-*k* candidates | A prompt for inspection and error analysis. | A causal account of a person’s preference. |
| Learned factors | A representation used by the model. | A verified identity, need, or metadata field. |

::: notes
Ask: “What would you inspect before making a claim about this model?” Listen for split protocol, candidate set, negative sampling, missing exposure, and examples of failure.
:::

## Scores Need Objectives

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="48%"}
### Prediction
How close is \(\hat r_{ui}\) to a numeric target?

Use when a score itself drives a decision; measures can include RMSE or MAE.
:::
::: {.column width="48%"}
### Ranking
Do useful items appear near the top of the visible list?

Use top-*k* measures such as NDCG@10 or Recall@10 for the declared task.
:::
:::

A latent-factor score is not enough: the **objective and metric decide what “better” means**.

::: notes
This compresses the former objectives section. Do not frame either prediction or ranking as universally superior; match the metric to the decision surface.
:::

## 🎰 Bandit Time: What Should a Home Screen Optimise? {background-color="#003D7C"}

<p class="bandit-question"><strong>A home screen must order ten candidate items for immediate display.</strong> Which measure most directly tests whether useful items appear near the top?</p>
<div class="bandit-options">
  <div class="bandit-option" style="border-color:#D32F2F"><strong>A.</strong> RMSE over predicted ratings.</div>
  <div class="bandit-option" style="border-color:#1976D2"><strong>B.</strong> NDCG@10.</div>
  <div class="bandit-option" style="border-color:#388E3C"><strong>C.</strong> The number of metadata tags per item.</div>
  <div class="bandit-option" style="border-color:#7B1FA2"><strong>D.</strong> The age of the user account.</div>
</div>
<p style="margin-top:.7em;color:#80cbc4;font-size:.73em;">Answer: <strong style="color:#ffffff;">B</strong>. NDCG@10 is position-sensitive; it assesses useful ordering in a displayed top-*k*.</p>

::: notes
Re-use the familiar activity treatment for an objective/metric check. Contrast A: it can be meaningful for a numeric prediction task but does not directly measure top-k order.
:::

## History Is Evidence, Not Preference

| Historical process | Model consequence | Question to ask |
|---|---|---|
| Uneven exposure | Sparse or distorted interaction evidence | Who had a genuine chance to interact? |
| Popularity reinforcement | Popular items receive stronger learned signals | Who receives repeated visibility? |
| Re-ranking for discovery | Today’s policy changes tomorrow’s data | Who gets a credible opportunity to be seen? |

<p style="margin-top:.8em;color:#EF7C00;font-weight:bold;">Use historical behaviour as evidence with limits—not as a neutral record of preference.</p>

::: notes
Retain the core ethical guardrail from the previous deck in a concise form. This supports the E1 bridge without attempting to reproduce the full former ethics activity.
:::

## E1 Bridge: Choose the Consequential Decision

For one approved recommendation surface, make a focused argument around one connected choice:

| Choice | Example question |
|---|---|
| Representation | Why use lexical features, latent factors, or both? |
| Objective | Why optimise a ranked list rather than numeric prediction? |
| Method | Why is BPR-MF, explicit MF, ALS, or another baseline appropriate? |
| Risk | How could missing exposure distort the interaction evidence? |

::: notes
Invite a focused technical argument, not a catalogue of all possible recommender components. Ask students to name the evidence that would support their choice.
:::

# Summary {background-color="#003D7C"}

## 🔑 <u>Representations Enable; Objectives Decide</u>

- **TF–IDF** represents lexical evidence; **dense embeddings** can generalise across learned contextual patterns.
- **LFM** represents user–item interaction patterns as learned factors—not identities or recorded metadata.
- **BPR** keeps the latent-factor idea but trains it for relative ranking under implicit feedback.
- A score or offline metric is useful evidence, never a complete account of user value or fairness.

<p style="margin-top:.8em;color:#EF7C00;font-weight:bold;">🔑 Better representation helps; responsible objectives and evaluation determine what the system actually delivers.</p>
::: notes
Close by restating the lecture’s through-line: representations make scoring possible, while evidence, objectives, and constraints decide whether a score is useful.
:::
